screens.title: Handling Events and Subscriptions
screens.subtitle: Real-time updates from smart contracts using web3.eth.subscribe

narration.text: In decentralized applications, being able to react quickly to on-chain changes is essential. In this lesson you will learn why smart contract events are a lightweight, efficient signal for off-chain software, and how persistent subscriptions replace costly polling. You will see how web3. eth. subscribe creates a continuous connection to an Ethereum node so your application can receive new block headers, pending transactions, or filtered logs for contract events. I will ground this with the practical example of monitoring an ERC-20 Transfer event: how to obtain the event signature, filter by contract address, decode the log data using the contract ABI, and update a UI in real time. We will also cover two operational concerns: handling connection drops and mitigating blockchain reorganizations by waiting for confirmations. By the end of this chapter you will understand the trade-offs between getPastEvents for historical state and subscriptions for live updates, and you will have a clear pattern for combining both safely. Consider how your dApp would behave if an event you relied on was later removed by a reorg — that question will guide many of the best practices you apply next.

keyIdea.title: Why events matter
keyIdea.text: Events are on-chain logs that let dApps react in real time without expensive polling. Subscriptions deliver these logs to your application as they happen.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: This chapter teaches four core competencies you will use when building live dApps. First, you will understand why real-time event handling is more efficient than polling: events are stored as logs and are designed for off-chain clients to react to contract changes. Second, you will distinguish one-time event polling from persistent subscriptions and decide when to use each pattern. Third, you will learn how to implement web3. eth. subscribe to receive new block headers, pending transactions, and logs, and how to decode event data using a contract ABI. Fourth, you will apply event filtering techniques so your application only processes relevant logs, improving performance and reducing cost. Each objective also includes a practical verification step, like wiring a React component to a WebSocket provider and validating that Transfer events are decoded correctly. As you work, keep one common misconception in mind: subscriptions do not make events final; you still need confirmation logic to handle possible blockchain reorganizations. These objectives set the foundation for the hands-on TokenMonitor activity later in the chapter.

keyIdea.title: Core competencies
keyIdea.text: Understand event logs, use subscriptions for live updates, decode events with an ABI, and apply filtering and confirmation strategies.

screens.title: Events as on-chain logs
screens.subtitle: What events are and why they are efficient for dApps

narration.text: Events are structured log entries a smart contract emits to signal that something important happened. Technically, these logs are stored in the transaction receipt and indexed in a way that makes off-chain clients efficient to query. In practice, this means a dApp can react to a Transfer, OwnershipTransferred, or other emitted event without re-reading every contract state variable repeatedly. For example, a marketplace UI can listen for a Sale event and update recent listings immediately, rather than polling the contract every few seconds. Events are lightweight because only the log and topics are stored and returned, not a full contract state snapshot. A common misconception is to treat events as a canonical source of truth for final state. Events are reliable records of what happened in a block, but they are still subject to blockchain reorganizations. That is, an event included in a block can become orphaned if a longer chain replaces that block. Therefore, while events provide excellent real-time signals, you should design your UX to show provisional state and confirm finality after a chosen number of block confirmations. When thinking about events, always decide which fields to index in Solidity to make efficient filtering possible later.

keyIdea.title: Events are logs
keyIdea.text: Events are stored as logs in transaction receipts and are optimized for off-chain consumption, not as a replacement for on-chain state verification.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Events as on-chain logs
Definition

Events are logs stored in receipts

Events are emitted by contracts to signal occurrences like transfers or state changes. They are stored as logs in the transaction receipt and can be filtered by topics.

  • Lightweight: only relevant fields and topics are returned.
  • Indexed parameters become topics for efficient filtering.
  • Not a replacement for reading final state; use confirmations.
Example
A Transfer event contains from, to, and value. An off-chain monitor decodes it and updates a recent transfers list.
Common mistake
Treating first-seen events as final without waiting for confirmations, which can be invalidated by reorgs.
Analogy

Events are like broadcast messages

Imagine a contract emitting a short bulletin instead of sending full state snapshots. Subscribers hear the bulletin and update local displays without asking for the full report.

Quick checklist
  • Decide which params to mark indexed in Solidity.
  • Design UI to show provisional vs final updates.
  • Record block number and transaction hash for finality checks.
Key Takeaway

Events are efficient signals for off-chain clients but require confirmation logic for finality.

screens.title: web3.eth.subscribe basics
screens.subtitle: Establishing persistent subscriptions with a WebSocket provider

narration.text: A subscription is a persistent channel between your dApp and an Ethereum node that delivers notifications as new data appears on-chain. To start, create a WebSocket provider and pass it to a Web3 instance. Then call web3. eth. subscribe with the subscription type you need — for example, 'newBlockHeaders' to receive block headers, 'pendingTransactions' to watch mempool activity, or 'logs' to receive contract events. Each subscription returns an object you can attach event handlers to, commonly 'data' and 'error'. In a React app, you should initialize the subscription inside a useEffect hook and return a cleanup function that unsubscribes and disconnects the provider. This pattern avoids memory leaks and ensures a tidy reconnection strategy. A practical pitfall is subscribing to high-volume feeds like pending transactions without filtering; such feeds can overwhelm clients and raise costs. Use filters when possible and consider batching or debouncing UI updates. Finally, remember subscriptions deliver events as they arrive, but they do not guarantee finality — treat incoming events as provisional until you verify a safe number of confirmations. web3.eth.subscribe basics means subscriptions using a websocket provider deliver continuous updates; manage lifecycle and filter aggressively to stay efficient.. In practical terms, establishing persistent subscriptions with a websocket provider. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Persistent channel
keyIdea.text: Subscriptions using a WebSocket provider deliver continuous updates; manage lifecycle and filter aggressively to stay efficient.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › web3.eth.subscribe basics
Quick pattern

Create provider → subscribe → handle → cleanup

Use a WebSocket provider with web3. Then call web3.eth.subscribe with type and filters. Attach .on('data') and .on('error') handlers to process incoming events.

Subscription types
  • newBlockHeaders: new blocks as they are mined.
  • pendingTransactions: mempool activity, high volume.
  • logs: contract events, filterable by address/topics.
Example
In a component, initialize the provider and subscribe in useEffect, and unsubscribe in the cleanup function to avoid dangling sockets.
Operational notes

Resilience and filtering

  • Filter subscriptions by contract address and topics to reduce noise.
  • Guard against high-volume streams like pendingTransactions unless you have batching.
  • Implement reconnect attempts and exponential backoff when the WS disconnects.
Key Takeaway

Subscriptions give live data; lifecycle and filtering are essential for a robust implementation.

screens.title: Subscriptions vs getPastEvents
screens.subtitle: When to use real-time subscriptions and when to perform historical queries

narration.text: It is important to choose the right tool for the job. Subscriptions are for live updates and are best when you need to react immediately to new events. getPastEvents is a one-time query that returns historical logs over a specified block range and is ideal for populating initial UI state or doing backfills. A common pattern is to call getPastEvents when the component mounts to load recent history, then establish a subscription to receive new events after that point. This hybrid approach gives both context and continuity. Consider trade-offs: historical queries can be slower and may be rate-limited, while subscriptions require a persistent connection and careful management of network instability. Another nuance: getPastEvents returns logs that are already part of the canonical chain at the time of the query, but they may still be subject to future reorgs if you query very recent blocks. A practical example is a token transfer list: use getPastEvents to fetch the last 100 transfers and then subscribe to Transfer logs to append new items in real time, while flagging newly received transfers as provisional until confirmations arrive.

keyIdea.title: Hybrid pattern
keyIdea.text: Combine getPastEvents for history and subscriptions for live updates to give users both context and immediacy.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Subscriptions vs getPastEvents
Subscriptions

Live stream for new events

  • Persistent WebSocket connection.
  • Delivers events as they happen.
  • Requires lifecycle and reconnection handling.
When to use
Real-time feeds, UI updates, and notifications.
getPastEvents

Historical queries

  • One-time RPC call for a block range.
  • Great for initial state or backfills.
  • May be slower and subject to rate limits.
When to use
Initial state loads, historical audits, and catch-up logic before subscribing.
Recommended hybrid flow
  1. Call getPastEvents to load recent history and populate UI.
  2. Establish a subscription to logs that start at the latest fetched block + 1.
  3. Mark incoming events as provisional until sufficient confirmations arrive.
Key Takeaway

Use a getPastEvents seed and then subscribe to logs for continuous updates while handling confirmations.

screens.title: Subscribing to Transfer events
screens.subtitle: Sample code to subscribe and decode Transfer logs

narration.text: Let's walk through the practical steps to subscribe to a Transfer event and decode the incoming log. First, initialize Web3 with a WebSocket provider. Next, get the event signature by hashing the event declaration; this is topic[0] and uniquely identifies the Transfer event. Then call web3. eth. subscribe('logs') with the token contract address and the signature as a topic filter. In the data handler you will receive a log object containing data, topics, transactionHash, and blockNumber. Use web3. eth. abi. decodeLog with the event inputs from the ABI to get named fields like from, to, and value. Handle errors from both the subscription and the decoder. A concrete example is a TokenMonitor component that appends decoded transfers to local state and keeps only the most recent entries for UI performance. Remember to unsubscribe in your cleanup and to disconnect the provider where supported. Also consider token decimals when converting raw uint256 values to human-readable amounts. Finally, always record the block number so you can implement confirmation logic separate from immediate UI updates. Subscribing to Transfer events means use the event signature as topic[0] and web3.eth.abi.decodelog to convert raw log data into typed fields for the ui.. In practical terms, sample code to subscribe and decode transfer logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Subscribe and decode
keyIdea.text: Use the event signature as topic[0] and web3.eth.abi.decodeLog to convert raw log data into typed fields for the UI.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Subscribing to Transfer events
Starter code
import Web3 from 'web3'

const web3 = new Web3(new Web3.providers.WebsocketProvider('wss://...'))
const tokenAbi = [ /* Transfer event ABI inputs */ ]
const tokenAddress = '0x...'
const sig = web3.utils.sha3('Transfer(address,address,uint256)')

web3.eth.subscribe('logs', { address: tokenAddress, topics: [sig] })
  .on('data', (log) => {
    const decoded = web3.eth.abi.decodeLog(tokenAbi[0].inputs, log.data, log.topics.slice(1))
    // decoded.from, decoded.to, decoded.value
  })
  .on('error', (err) => console.error('Subscription error', err))

Keep the code readable, convert values using token decimals, and store blockNumber for confirmation checks.

Explanation
  • sig is topic[0] and filters to Transfer events only.
  • decodeLog maps raw data to named fields using the ABI inputs.
  • log.topics.slice(1) are indexed parameters like from and to when marked indexed.
Example
When a Transfer arrives, decode and push a short object {from,to,value,blockNumber} into UI state to render immedately.
Pitfall
Assuming value uses 18 decimals. Always confirm token decimals before converting raw units.

screens.title: Event signature and topics
screens.subtitle: How event topic[0] and indexed parameters enable efficient filtering

narration.text: An event signature is the keccak-256 hash of the event name and its parameter types; in logs it appears as topic[0] and uniquely identifies an event type. Parameters declared as indexed in Solidity become additional topics, allowing logs to be filtered by those values without decoding all logs. For example, a Transfer event with two indexed addresses will place the sender and recipient in topics[1] and topics[2], which lets you subscribe to transfers from or to specific addresses efficiently. This mechanism is critical because the chain emits a huge amount of logs and you only want relevant ones. When constructing a subscription, supply the event signature as the first topic and optionally include specific indexed parameter hashes or null to accept any. A misconception is to try to filter by non-indexed parameters at the subscription level — that is not possible; non-indexed fields are only present in the data payload and must be decoded after receipt. In practice, design which parameters to index carefully during contract design: indexing increases filterability but also consumes more log space. For monitoring, always record topics and the raw data so you can re-decode if additional context is needed later.

keyIdea.title: Topics enable filtering
keyIdea.text: Use topic[0] for event identity and indexed topics for efficient address or value matching; non-indexed data must be decoded from log.data.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Event signature & topics
Core idea

topic[0] = keccak(event declaration)

The event name and parameter types are hashed to form the event signature that appears as the first topic in logs.

Indexed params → topics
Parameters declared indexed appear in topics and can be used as subscription filters without decoding the data payload.
Practical filter examples
Filter for all Transfer events: topics: [sig]
Filter for transfers to a specific address: topics: [sig, null, fromAddressHash]
Cannot filter by non-indexed value at subscription time — decode first, then filter in app logic.
Key Takeaway

Plan indexes during contract design and use topics to minimize the volume of logs your app processes.

screens.title: Decoding logs with an ABI
screens.subtitle: Turn raw log data into readable fields

narration.text: Decoding a log is straightforward once you have the event ABI inputs. The web3. eth. abi. decodeLog function accepts the inputs array, the log. data string, and an array of topic values for indexed parameters. It returns an object with named fields matching your event parameters. For an ERC-20 Transfer event, you will receive a decoded object with from, to, and value fields; the value is returned as a string representing the raw integer amount. A clear example: when a Transfer log arrives, decode it and then convert value to a human-friendly token amount using the token's decimals. Always wrap decode operations in try/catch because malformed logs or unexpected ABI mismatches can throw. Also persist the original log's blockNumber and transactionHash so you can later verify finality or re-decode if necessary. One misconception is to decode using a mismatched ABI; the mapping between inputs and data must match exactly. Keep the contract ABI for the events you expect available client-side or derive the necessary inputs during build time. Decoding logs with an ABI means use decodelog with abi inputs and topics to map raw log data to named parameters, then convert units with decimals and store provenance data.. In practical terms, turn raw log data into readable fields. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decode reliably
keyIdea.text: Use decodeLog with ABI inputs and topics to map raw log data to named parameters, then convert units with decimals and store provenance data.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Decoding logs with an ABI
Decoder pattern
try {
  const decoded = web3.eth.abi.decodeLog(abiInputs, log.data, log.topics.slice(1))
  // decoded.from, decoded.to, decoded.value
} catch (e) {
  console.error('Decode failed', e, log)
}

Store blockNumber and transactionHash with the decoded result so you can check confirmations and provenance later.

Conversion & validation
  • Convert raw uint256 using token decimals to display human amounts.
  • Validate decoded fields and handle any ABI mismatches gracefully.
  • Keep original log for retry or forensic needs.
Key Takeaway

Decoding maps opaque log bytes into meaningful fields; always handle conversion and save provenance data.

screens.title: Connection resilience and cleanup
screens.subtitle: Practical patterns to handle disconnects and unmounts

narration.text: WebSocket connections can drop unexpectedly, so handling reconnections and cleaning up subscriptions is essential. In a React component, initialize your Web3 provider and subscription inside a useEffect hook. Save the subscription object and the provider reference so you can unsubscribe and disconnect when the component unmounts. Use a retry strategy with exponential backoff for reconnection attempts, and limit retries to avoid tight reconnect loops. When re-establishing subscriptions after a disconnect, consider the last processed block number and request past events for the gap to avoid missing any logs. Another pattern is to tag incoming events as provisional until you have processed confirmations; that way a reconnection or reorg won't incorrectly mark items as final. A common mistake is to leave subscriptions active when components unmount, causing memory leaks and duplicate event processing. Finally, log connection lifecycle events for easier debugging and monitoring in production. Connection resilience and cleanup means always unsubscribe and disconnect providers on cleanup, and implement a reconnection strategy that backfills missed blocks to avoid gaps.. In practical terms, practical patterns to handle disconnects and unmounts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle management
keyIdea.text: Always unsubscribe and disconnect providers on cleanup, and implement a reconnection strategy that backfills missed blocks to avoid gaps.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Connection resilience
Lifecycle pattern
  1. Init provider and subscription inside useEffect.
  2. Store subscription ref so you can unsubscribe later.
  3. On unmount, call subscription.unsubscribe and disconnect provider if supported.
Reconnection
Implement retry with exponential backoff and on reconnect fetch past events for any missed block range.
Practical checklist
  • Limit subscription scope with address/topics.
  • Debounce UI updates to avoid rendering storms.
  • Persist last processed block to resume safely after reconnect.
Key Takeaway

Graceful cleanup and reconnection with backfill are essential to avoid lost or duplicated events.

screens.title: Blockchain reorganizations (reorgs)
screens.subtitle: Why reorgs matter and how they affect events

narration.text: A blockchain reorganization happens when a previously accepted block is replaced by a different block because a longer chain was discovered. For applications that react to events, a reorg can mean an event you saw earlier disappears from the canonical chain. That is why treating first-seen events as final is risky. To mitigate, many dApps wait for a certain number of confirmations — additional blocks mined on top of the block containing the event — before marking an event as final. The typical confirmation range depends on your risk tolerance; for many applications, waiting for six confirmations is a common compromise between speed and safety. When a reorg occurs, your subscription may emit logs from the new chain; your application should detect that an event's block is no longer part of the canonical chain by comparing block hashes and numbers or re-querying the node. For critical flows, consider building a reconciliation step that compares the app's state to on-chain data periodically and corrects any discrepancies caused by reorgs. The key is to design both user-facing messaging and backend reconciliation with reorgs in mind.

keyIdea.title: Reorgs reverse events
keyIdea.text: Reorgs can orphan previously seen events. Use confirmations and reconciliation logic to avoid incorrect final state updates.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Blockchain reorganizations
What is a reorg?

A reorg replaces a previously accepted block with a different block when a longer chain appears. Events in the orphaned block no longer exist in the canonical chain.

Symptoms for dApps
Transactions or events shown as confirmed disappear later, causing UI inconsistencies.
Mitigations
  • Wait for N confirmations before marking events final.
  • Record block hashes and re-verify chain inclusion if needed.
  • Run periodic reconciliation comparing stored state with on-chain queries.
Key Takeaway

Design for provisional updates and reconciliation so reorgs do not leave your application in an incorrect state.

screens.title: TokenMonitor lab walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Combining getPastEvents and subscribe to display live transfers

narration.text: In the hands-on TokenMonitor lab you will build a small React component that combines historical loading and a live subscription. First, call getPastEvents to fetch recent Transfer logs for the token and populate your state with decoded entries. Record the highest block number you saw. Then initialize a WebSocket provider and subscribe to logs with topic[0] equal to the Transfer signature, starting from the next block after your last fetched block. In the subscription data handler decode each incoming log and prepend it to the UI list, marking it as provisional until it reaches your configured confirmation threshold. Implement cleanup in the useEffect return to unsubscribe and disconnect the provider, and add a reconnection strategy that backfills any missed blocks using getPastEvents between the last processed block and the current head. This lab reinforces practical concerns: token decimals, unique keys for list items using transactionHash plus logIndex, and avoiding duplicate entries. After completing the lab, test a reorg scenario by simulating a late block replacement and verify your reconciliation logic corrects the UI accordingly. TokenMonitor lab walkthrough means seed ui with getpastevents, subscribe to logs for live updates, mark provisional events, and reconcile on reconnect or reorgs.. In practical terms, combining getpastevents and subscribe to display live transfers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Filtering pitfalls and best practices
screens.subtitle: Avoiding noisy subscriptions and incorrect assumptions

narration.text: Filtering is powerful but easy to misuse. The biggest pitfall is subscribing to broad feeds like pendingTransactions or logs without narrowing by address or topic, which can overwhelm clients with irrelevant data. Always specify the contract address and the event signature when possible. Another trap is attempting to filter by non-indexed fields at subscription time — only indexed fields appear in topics and can be used as filters. If you need to narrow by non-indexed fields, you must decode logs and filter in application logic after receipt. Also be careful with topic ordering: topics in the filter correspond to indexed parameter positions. When building a UI, debounce or batch updates so a burst of incoming events doesn't cause rendering performance problems. Finally, handle decode exceptions and unexpected ABI changes; if the contract ABI changes you may receive logs you cannot decode correctly. The best practice is to log unexpected logs for later analysis and avoid crashing the subscription handler. These steps will keep your subscription efficient and resilient. Filtering pitfalls and best practices means specify address and topic filters; decode non-indexed fields in the app and batch ui updates to prevent overload.. In practical terms, avoiding noisy subscriptions and incorrect assumptions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Filter carefully
keyIdea.text: Specify address and topic filters; decode non-indexed fields in the app and batch UI updates to prevent overload.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Filtering pitfalls

Common errors

  • Subscribing to broad topics like pendingTransactions without a filter.
  • Expecting to filter by non-indexed data at subscription time.
  • Not handling ABI mismatches which break decode logic.
Performance tip
Batch or debounce UI updates when many events arrive quickly to reduce re-renders.

Failure handling

When decoding fails or an unexpected log arrives, log the raw payload and continue. Crashing the handler will stop receiving future events.

Key Takeaway

Filter down to what you need, handle decode errors gracefully, and avoid rendering storms for large volumes.

narration.text: Here are the essential ideas to keep in mind when implementing event-driven dApps. First, events are logs emitted by smart contracts and are optimized for off-chain consumption; they are not a direct replacement for reading on-chain state. Second, subscriptions using web3. eth. subscribe provide real-time delivery but require lifecycle and reconnection handling. Third, event filtering relies on the event signature and indexed topics; non-indexed fields must be decoded from the data payload. These concepts together shape a reliable pattern: seed your UI with historical events, subscribe for live updates, decode and convert values with the correct decimals, and wait for confirmations before treating events as final. Keep these core ideas handy as you build so your applications remain responsive and correct even when facing network flakiness or chain reorganizations. Key Concepts means events are logs, subscriptions are live channels, and topics enable filterability — combine these with confirmations for reliable uis.. In practical terms, what to remember. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Three essentials
keyIdea.text: Events are logs, subscriptions are live channels, and topics enable filterability — combine these with confirmations for reliable UIs.

Events

Subscriptions

Topics

Summary
Combine historical queries with live subscriptions, decode logs with an ABI, filter by topics, and implement confirmation and reconnection strategies to build reliable real-time dApps.

narration.text: Use this checklist as you implement event-driven features. First, always include the contract address and the correct event signature as your subscription filters. Second, decode logs using the ABI and convert numeric values with the token's decimals before displaying them. Third, design lifecycle and confirmation handling: unsubscribe on cleanup, reconnect with backfill, and wait for confirmations before treating changes as final. These three practical reminders will keep your TokenMonitor responsive, correct, and resilient to network issues or chain reorganizations. When in doubt, prefer a conservative confirmation count and instrument your app to reconcile periodically against on-chain queries. Key Concepts — Practical checklist means filter by address/signature, decode and convert values correctly, and manage lifecycle plus confirmation/backfill logic.. In practical terms, compact reminders for implementation. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Practical checklist
Filter
Use contract address and event signature to limit results.
Decode
Use the event ABI to decode data and convert units with decimals.
Confirm & reconcile
Wait for confirmations, backfill on reconnect, and periodically reconcile state with the chain.
Final reminder
These practical checks keep live event handling efficient and correct in the face of connectivity issues and reorgs.

ai_generation_note: Create a 12-minute live coding video demonstrating real-time event handling. Start with a basic React component, then integrate Web3.js to subscribe to `Transfer` events from a public ERC-20 token on Sepolia testnet. Show the `web3.eth.subscribe('logs')` setup, how to get the event signature, decode the incoming `log.data`, and update the React component's state to display new transfers. Include a split-screen view of the code editor and the browser console/UI updating as new events come in. Emphasize the use of a WebSocket provider and the importance of `useEffect` cleanup. Briefly explain reorgs with a simple diagram overlay. End with a 2-question interactive mini-quiz on event filtering and reorgs.
